blocks.text: On the fifth morning after a sigmoid colectomy, a 68-year-old man who had been progressing well stops eating his breakfast. His temperature is 38.2 degrees C, his heart rate 112/min, and the nurse mentions that his drain has turned cloudy and brown. A rising pulse on postoperative day 5 is a finding that must never be explained away, because it can be the first sign that the join in the bowel has failed.

blocks.markdown: Postoperative care has three tasks: replace what the patient cannot take by mouth (fluids and nutrition), keep them comfortable enough to breathe, cough and mobilise (analgesia), and detect complications early (monitoring). The surgical stress response causes salt and water retention, so patients tend to retain fluid for the first 24 to 48 hours; over-prescribing saline is a frequent iatrogenic error causing oedema, ileus and delayed healing.

blocks.title: Maintenance fluid requirements
blocks.text: For an adult who is nil by mouth and not otherwise losing fluid, daily maintenance needs are approximately 25 to 30 mL/kg of water, about 1 mmol/kg of each of sodium, potassium and chloride, and 50 to 100 g of glucose to limit starvation ketosis (as in NICE guidance on intravenous fluids). Replace abnormal losses (drains, stoma, vomiting, fever, third-space) separately and review at least daily.

blocks.title: Prescribing 24-hour maintenance fluid
blocks.prompt: A 72 kg patient is nil by mouth on the first postoperative day with no abnormal losses and normal renal function. Calculate their approximate water, sodium and potassium requirements and choose an appropriate fluid.

steps.text: Sodium and potassium: about 1 mmol/kg/day each.

Choose a balanced regimen such as 0.18% saline with 4% glucose (sodium about 30 mmol/L, glucose 40 g/L) with potassium chloride added; 1.8 L supplies about 54 mmol sodium and 72 g glucose, within the target range.
Check urea, electrolytes and fluid balance daily and adjust; stop intravenous fluids as soon as oral intake is adequate.

blocks.answer: About 1.8 L water, around 72 mmol each of sodium and potassium, and 50 to 100 g glucose over 24 hours, reviewed daily.

blocks.markdown: **Analgesia.** Effective analgesia is multimodal: regular paracetamol, an NSAID if there is no contraindication (renal impairment, peptic ulcer, bleeding risk, heart failure), and an opioid for moderate to severe pain, given by patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) or as needed. Regional techniques (epidural, nerve blocks, local anaesthetic infiltration) reduce opioid use. Co-prescribe a laxative and antiemetic with opioids and monitor sedation and respiratory rate. Poorly controlled pain causes splinting, atelectasis, immobility and thromboembolic risk.

blocks.caption: Postoperative fever by timing
rows: Surgical stress and inflammatory response, atelectasis, transfusion reaction, drug fever
Urinary tract infection (catheter), pneumonia, cannula phlebitis
Dysuria, cough, purulent sputum, tender cannula site
Surgical site infection, anastomotic leak, intra-abdominal collection, deep vein thrombosis
Wound erythema, tachycardia, abdominal pain, calf swelling
Abscess, collection, drug reaction, pulmonary embolism, Clostridioides difficile

blocks.title: Reasoning from fever timing
blocks.prompt: A 55-year-old woman, day 6 after a right hemicolectomy, has a temperature of 38.6 degrees C, heart rate 108/min, a distended tender abdomen, and CRP rising from 120 to 260 mg/L. Her wound looks clean. Which causes are most important to exclude?

steps.text: Timing: day 6 lies in the period of surgical site infection, anastomotic leak, collection and DVT.
Clean wound makes superficial wound infection less likely.
Rising CRP, tachycardia and abdominal findings point to intra-abdominal sepsis, specifically anastomotic leak.
Therefore request urgent senior review and contrast CT of abdomen and pelvis; resuscitate and start antibiotics; surgery if unstable or peritonitic.

blocks.answer: Most important is anastomotic leak with intra-abdominal sepsis: resuscitation, antibiotics, CT, and surgical review for re-laparotomy or drainage.

blocks.markdown: **Anastomotic leak** typically declares itself between days 3 and 7 with tachycardia, fever, abdominal pain or distension, ileus, rising CRP, new confusion or enteric content in the drain. **Wound infection** produces erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness and discharge at days 5 to 7; treatment is opening and draining the wound, with antibiotics if there is spreading cellulitis or systemic signs. **Venous thromboembolism (VTE)** includes deep vein thrombosis (unilateral calf swelling, pain, warmth) and pulmonary embolism (pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypoxia). Risk is raised by surgery, immobility, cancer and age. Prophylaxis uses early mobilisation, graduated or intermittent compression and, in most major surgery, low molecular weight heparin unless contraindicated.

blocks.caption: Recognising three key complications
rows: Tachycardia, fever, abdominal pain, ileus, drain contents
Examine wound, open and drain, antibiotics if cellulitis
Calf swelling, pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, hypoxia
Risk score, imaging, therapeutic anticoagulation per local policy

blocks.title: Unexplained tachycardia
blocks.text: Unexplained tachycardia, new confusion or falling urine output after abdominal surgery should be treated as evidence of bleeding, sepsis or leak until proven otherwise. Use early warning scores to trigger review, and do not attribute changes to 'pain' or 'ileus' without a senior assessment.

items: Fluids: maintenance of about 25 to 30 mL/kg/day water plus replacement of losses; avoid routine excess saline.
Analgesia: regular paracetamol, NSAID if safe, opioid for severe pain with laxative and antiemetic.
Fever: ask what day it is, then think of lungs, urine, wound, leak, veins.
VTE: prophylaxis by mobilisation, compression and low molecular weight heparin for most major surgery.

points: Maintenance fluids are about 25 to 30 mL/kg/day water with about 1 mmol/kg each of sodium and potassium and 50 to 100 g glucose, adjusted for losses.
Postoperative analgesia is multimodal and opioids need a laxative and monitoring.
Fever is differentiated by timing: early stress response or atelectasis, then urine and chest, then wound, leak and thrombosis.
Anastomotic leak, wound infection and VTE have characteristic timing and features, and unexplained tachycardia demands senior review.

questions.stem: Which regimen best matches the standard maintenance requirement for a 70 kg adult who is nil by mouth for 24 hours?

options.text: About 1.75 to 2.1 L water with about 70 mmol each of sodium and potassium and 50 to 100 g glucose
3 L of 0.9% saline plus 100 mmol potassium

questions.correctOptionText: About 1.75 to 2.1 L water with about 70 mmol each of sodium and potassium and 50 to 100 g glucose

distractorRationale.a: Correct: 25 to 30 mL/kg water and about 1 mmol/kg each electrolyte.
distractorRationale.b: Far too much fluid and sodium.
distractorRationale.c: Far too little water and no electrolytes.

questions.explanation: Maintenance is calculated per kilogram: 25 to 30 mL/kg of water and about 1 mmol/kg each of sodium, potassium and chloride, plus 50 to 100 g glucose. For 70 kg this gives about 1.75 to 2.1 L and 70 mmol of each ion.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old patient with acute kidney injury (creatinine doubled) has moderate pain on postoperative day 1. Which analgesic strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Regular paracetamol with a carefully titrated opioid, avoiding NSAIDs, plus a laxative
No analgesia to avoid masking signs

questions.correctOptionText: Regular paracetamol with a carefully titrated opioid, avoiding NSAIDs, plus a laxative

distractorRationale.a: Correct: multimodal analgesia that avoids nephrotoxic NSAIDs.
distractorRationale.c: Untreated pain causes splinting and complications.
distractorRationale.d: Opioids require monitoring and a laxative.

questions.explanation: Multimodal analgesia combines simple analgesics and opioids for greater effect with lower opioid doses. NSAIDs are avoided with kidney injury, and opioids are titrated with monitoring in renal impairment because metabolites accumulate.

questions.stem: A patient has a temperature of 37.9 degrees C on the evening after a laparotomy, with otherwise normal observations and a clean wound. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The surgical stress response with or without early atelectasis

questions.correctOptionText: The surgical stress response with or without early atelectasis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: early low-grade fever commonly reflects cytokine response or atelectasis.
distractorRationale.c: Abscesses present later with swinging fever.
distractorRationale.d: Wound infection takes days to develop.

questions.explanation: Low-grade fever within 48 hours of surgery is usually the inflammatory response to tissue injury, sometimes with atelectasis. Infective causes such as wound infection and leak appear later.

questions.stem: On day 4 after an inguinal hernia repair under general anaesthesia with a urinary catheter, a patient has temperature 38.3 degrees C, suprapubic discomfort and cloudy urine. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: timing and urinary symptoms in a catheterised patient.
distractorRationale.b: Atelectasis typically occurs in the first two days and has chest signs.
distractorRationale.d: Malignant hyperthermia occurs during or just after anaesthesia.

questions.explanation: Fever around day 3 to 5 with urinary symptoms in a catheterised patient points to urinary infection. Differentiation by timing and associated features guides targeted investigation.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman on day 8 after an open incisional hernia repair has sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, SpO2 89% on air, heart rate 120/min and a swollen left calf. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Give oxygen, assess risk, arrange CT pulmonary angiography and start therapeutic anticoagulation if there will be delay and no contraindication
Reassure that this is atelectasis and discharge

questions.correctOptionText: Give oxygen, assess risk, arrange CT pulmonary angiography and start therapeutic anticoagulation if there will be delay and no contraindication

distractorRationale.a: Correct: suspected PE with DVT signs needs oxygen, imaging and early anticoagulation.
distractorRationale.b: Hypoxia and tachycardia are not benign.
distractorRationale.c: Anticoagulation is the treatment, not something to stop without assessing bleeding risk.

questions.explanation: Pleuritic pain, hypoxia, tachycardia and calf swelling after surgery strongly suggest pulmonary embolism from DVT. Confirm with CTPA, and anticoagulate promptly unless bleeding risk contraindicates it.

questions.stem: Anastomotic leak usually presents within the first 24 hours after surgery.
questions.explanation: Leaks typically appear between days 3 and 7, as the anastomosis passes through its weakest healing phase. Early tachycardia or collapse in the first day is more suggestive of bleeding or technical failure.

questions.stem: An 84 kg patient is nil by mouth. Using 25 mL/kg/day of maintenance water, calculate the hourly infusion rate (mL/h), assuming no abnormal losses.
questions.explanation: Daily water is 25 x 84 = 2100 mL, and dividing by 24 hours gives 87.5 mL/h. This is a starting rate to be reviewed against losses, urine output and electrolytes.

questions.stem: A 70 kg patient receives 2 litres of 0.9% sodium chloride (154 mmol/L of sodium) in 24 hours. Using a maintenance target of 1 mmol/kg/day, by how many mmol does the sodium delivered exceed the maintenance target?
questions.explanation: Sodium delivered is 2 x 154 = 308 mmol, while the target is 1 x 70 = 70 mmol, so the excess is 308 - 70 = 238 mmol. This illustrates why routine large volumes of 0.9% saline produce sodium and water overload in the postoperative period.

questions.stem: A patient develops a fever on the third day after major abdominal surgery. Explain how the day of onset helps you choose likely causes and what you would examine.
markingGuide: Day 0 to 2: stress response, atelectasis, transfusion reaction, drug fever
Day 3 to 5: urinary tract infection, pneumonia, cannula site infection
Day 5 to 7: surgical site infection, anastomotic leak, collection, DVT
Later: abscess, drug fever, C. difficile, PE
Examine chest, urine and catheter, cannula sites, wound, abdomen, calves
Investigations: FBC, CRP, cultures, urinalysis, chest radiograph, CT as indicated
questions.explanation: Fever causes cluster by time because each pathological process needs a characteristic interval to develop. Using timing narrows the differential and focuses examination and tests.

questions.stem: Describe how you would recognise and initially manage (a) an anastomotic leak, (b) a wound infection and (c) venous thromboembolism in a postoperative patient.
markingGuide: Leak: day 3 to 7, tachycardia, fever, abdominal pain or distension, ileus, rising CRP, drain contents
Leak management: resuscitation, antibiotics, contrast CT, senior surgical review, drainage or re-laparotomy
Wound infection: day 5 to 7, erythema, warmth, tenderness, discharge
Wound management: open and drain, swab, antibiotics if cellulitis or systemic signs
VTE: calf swelling or pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, tachycardia, hypoxia
VTE management: risk assessment, imaging (Doppler ultrasound or CTPA), therapeutic anticoagulation
Prevention: mobilisation, compression, low molecular weight heparin
questions.explanation: Each complication has typical timing, symptoms and signs that allow early recognition. Early treatment reduces mortality, particularly in leak and pulmonary embolism.
